cards.title: Read the address
cards.body:
A fake site can copy a logo. It can't copy the real address. The owner is the name just before the **very last ending** (like `.example`, `.com` or `.com.au`).

- `login.yourbank.example` is Your Bank's: only the owner can add things in front.
- `yourbank.example.login-check.example` belongs to **login-check.example**.
- `yourbank-secure.example` is a [[lookalike|lookalike-domain]]. So is `yourbnak.example`: one swapped letter, zero honesty.

cards.prompt: Your Bank's site is `yourbank.example`. Find the **very last ending**, then the name just before it. Anything after a `/` is just a page. Which addresses really belong to Your Bank?
cards.explanation: `yourbank.example/signin` and `login.yourbank.example` both end in `yourbank.example`, so they're Your Bank's. `yourbank-secure.example` and `yourbnak.example` are lookalikes: the name before the ending isn't exactly `yourbank`.
cards.hint: For each one, find the very last ending and read the name just before it. Is that name exactly `yourbank`?
cards.nudge: Only the name just before the very last ending counts. A different word, extra letters or swapped letters means a different owner.

cards.prompt: The padlock next to an address means your connection is **encrypted**: nobody can read what you send on the way. This page has a padlock, and it asks for your card PIN. What does the padlock tell you?

options.text: That the PIN can't be read on the way, whoever gets it
That the site has been checked, so asking for a PIN is fine
options.nudge: Nobody checks a site's honesty before it gets a padlock. It's about the trip, not who's at the other end.

options.text: That it's really your bank's page, since scam sites can't get one
options.nudge: Scam sites can get a padlock too. Think about what encryption protects, and what it doesn't.

cards.explanation: The padlock means the connection is **encrypted**, so nobody can read it on the way. It says nothing about who runs the site: scam sites can have one too. And a bank never asks for your PIN on a website.
cards.hint: Encryption protects your data on the trip. Does it tell you who is waiting at the other end?

cards.prompt: You opened this page from a link in a text. Your Bank's real site is `yourbank.example`. A sign-in page asks for your username and password, but a bank **never** asks for your card PIN. Tap **every** warning sign.
cards.explanation: Three warning signs: the address belongs to `login-check.example` (the **wrong owner**), the banner is **rushing you**, and it **asks for your card PIN**. The padlock and the logo look real, but they don't prove anything.
cards.hint: Read the address to find its owner. Then look for pressure, and for a secret a bank would never ask for.
cards.nudge: Three things on this page match warning signs you know: who owns the address, pressure, and a secret. Look for each in turn.

cards.prompt: A **password manager** only fills in your password on the real site. You tap a link in an email to sign in to your game account.

steps.text: The page looks right, but your **password manager doesn't offer to fill in** your password. What might that mean?

choices.text: This might not be the real site
choices.consequence: Good thinking. A password manager only fills in on the real address.

choices.text: The password manager is broken, so type it in
choices.consequence: The manager is working: it didn't recognise the address. Typing it in hands it over.

choices.text: Close the page, then open the game's app or type the address yourself
choices.consequence: Safe. If there was really something to sign in for, you'll see it there.

choices.text: Type it in just once, to check
choices.consequence: Once is enough for a fake site to keep your password.

cards.explanation: A quiet password manager is a clue that the address isn't the real one. Don't sign in from a link: use the **app, a bookmark or the typed address**.
cards.hint: Where does a password manager fill in passwords? What's the safe way to reach an account?

cards.prompt: Oops. Before you noticed, you typed your bank password and card number into a fake site.

steps.text: What do you do about the password?

choices.text: Wait and see if anything strange happens
choices.consequence: Waiting gives the scammer time to use it. Fast is what counts.

choices.text: Change it straight away, and tell a trusted adult
choices.consequence: Now the stolen password is useless. And it's not your fault: fake sites fool adults too.

steps.text: Now the card. Which number do you call?

choices.text: The help number shown on the fake page
choices.consequence: That number belongs to the scammers. Use one you found yourself.

choices.text: The number on the card, or on the bank's official website
choices.consequence: The bank can stop the card before anyone uses it.

cards.explanation: Typed details into a fake site? **Change that password straight away** and tell a trusted adult. For a bank card, call the bank on the number **on the card or its official website**, never one from the fake page.
cards.hint: What makes a stolen password useless? And where can you find a bank's number that a scammer didn't give you?

cards.prompt: Which address really belongs to Your Bank (`yourbank.example`)?

options.nudge: Find the very last ending, then the name just before it: `help-centre`. So help-centre.example owns it.
`yourbank-help` is a different name from `yourbank`: a lookalike.
`help-yourbank` isn't `yourbank`. Only the exact name before the ending counts.

cards.explanation: `help.yourbank.example` ends in `yourbank.example`, so it's Your Bank's: only the owner can add `help.` in front. The others belong to someone else.
cards.hint: For each address, find the very last ending, then the name just before it.

cards.prompt: Label four things on this page.
cards.explanation: The address has the **wrong owner**, the banner is **rushing you**, the page **asks for your PIN**, and the padlock **only means encrypted**: it doesn't make the site real.
cards.hint: Match each label to one part of the page. One label is about something that looks reassuring but proves nothing.
cards.nudge: Each label is something you learned about fake sign-in pages. Take one at a time and find the part it describes.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- The owner is the name **just before the very last ending**.
- A **padlock only means encrypted**. Scam sites can have one.
- Sign in through the **app, a bookmark or a typed address**.

That's scams covered. Next: keeping your private stuff private.
